statement: When the two digits of a certain two-digit number are swapped, the new number is 27 bigger. How many two-digit numbers have this property?

choices.misconception: I found that the units digit must be 3 more than the tens digit and gave that 3 as the answer.
I listed 14, 25, 36, 47 and 58 and stopped too soon, missing 69.
I also counted 03, which becomes 30, but 03 is not a two-digit number.
I counted every two-digit number whose digits differ by 3, including those that get smaller when swapped.

hints: Write the number as 10 times the tens digit plus the units digit.
Work out how much a number changes when its digits swap, in terms of its two digits. The change has a simple form that tells you how the digits must be related. Then list every number that fits.
Swapping changes the number by 9 times the difference of the digits, so the units digit must be exactly 3 more than the tens digit, and the tens digit cannot be 0.

solutions.reliable: Call the tens digit a and the units digit b, so the number is 10a + b. Swapped, it is 10b + a. The increase is (10b + a) - (10a + b) = 9b - 9a = 9 x (b - a). This must be 27, so b - a = 3. The tens digit a must be at least 1 and b at most 9, so a can be 1 to 6: 14, 25, 36, 47, 58, 69. That is 6 numbers. Check one: 41 - 14 = 27. The transferable idea: swapping two digits always changes a number by 9 times the difference of the digits.
solutions.elegant: Try one: 14 becomes 41, which is 27 bigger. Adding 11 raises both digits by 1 and keeps the gap of 3, so the list is 14, 25, 36, and so on up to 69, where the units digit reaches 9. That is 6 numbers.

whyOnTest: Digit puzzles reward writing a number as 10a + b; the rule that a swap changes a number by 9 times the digit gap comes up again and again.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
